theme: “I know that my Redeemer lives”; the friends harden
readingInstruction: Read Job 14:1-17:16. Job reflects on the brevity of life, Eliphaz returns with a harsher speech, and Job answers by looking toward heaven for a witness. Read the speeches for the fragments of hope that keep breaking through.
settingTheScene: The first round of speeches is over, and the second begins. The friends are getting harder, not softer. Eliphaz tells Job that his own mouth condemns him, and he spends a whole chapter describing the miserable life of the wicked, which is a pointed way of saying that Job is suffering because he is wicked. Job’s replies show someone who is wearing out. He has no hope in his friends and almost none in this life. But in the middle of the despair, he reaches for something he can hardly name: a witness in heaven.
observation: Job says, “Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble” (14:1).
He compares a person to a tree: “For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again” (14:7), but man “lies down and rises not again” (14:12).
He asks, “If a man dies, shall he live again?” (14:14), and then expresses a hope that God would hide him in Sheol until his wrath has passed and then remember him.
Eliphaz accuses Job: “Your own mouth condemns you, and not I” (15:6).
Eliphaz describes the wicked man as one who “writhes in pain all his days” (15:20).
Job calls them “miserable comforters” (16:2) and says that God has worn him out (16:7).
Job says, “Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high” (16:19).
He pleads, “O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place” (16:18).
In chapter 17 he asks God to “lay down a pledge for me with yourself; who is there who will put up security for me?” (17:3).
interpretation:
The first thing to notice is that Job’s questions are about more than his own pain. In chapter 14 he thinks about human life in general. We are short-lived, like a flower, and we are fragile. A tree that is cut down can sprout again from the stump. A person who dies seems to have no such hope. This is the darkest thought in the chapter, and it presses on Job until he asks the question that the rest of the Old Testament will slowly answer: “If a man dies, shall he live again?”

Then Job does something remarkable. He imagines that the answer could be yes. “All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come” (14:14). He pictures God hiding him in Sheol like a man put away until a storm passes, and then calling to him. “You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands” (14:15). Job is not stating a doctrine of resurrection. He is imagining a possibility, and he is aware that it is a longing and not a certainty. But the longing is there, and it will grow.

Eliphaz’s second speech has no such moment. He is stuck in his system and he hardens. He says Job’s own mouth proves his guilt. He gives a long picture of the fate of the wicked. Notice that Eliphaz is not entirely wrong about the general truth. But it has become a trap for him and for Job.

Job’s answer in chapter 16 contains a shift. He first says that God is against him, which is where the pain is sharpest. But then, in 16:19, he turns to heaven. “My witness is in heaven.” He does not know who this witness is. It is another longing, like the arbiter of 9:33. Job has been wishing for someone who can speak for him before God. Now he is saying that such a person exists. God himself, in some mysterious way, will be Job’s advocate against God. It is a paradox and he does not resolve it.

Chapter 17 picks up the same thought. Job asks God to put up security for him, because no one else will. Only God can stand surety for Job against God.
connection: Paul will say that Christ’s resurrection answers Job’s question: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). 1 John 2:1 says, “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” Hebrews 7:22 says that Jesus became “the guarantor of a better covenant,” the surety Job longed for.
application:
Spend time today thinking about the shortness of life. It can be a gift when it moves you to trust God, and it can be a burden when you use it as a reason to despair. Ask which one it is for you.

Remember that Jesus is the witness in heaven, the advocate, and the one who stood surety for you. Thank him specifically, and name something you needed an advocate for.

If you are tired of “miserable comforters,” ask God to send you a faithful friend, and ask him to make you one.
prayerPrompts: Tell God how worn out you are, if you are.
Thank Jesus that because he lives, you will live.
Ask him to send you comfort, and to make you a comfort to someone else.
